Awaiting trial

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
of the 161 000 prisoner in South Africa 44 000 of them are awaiting trial and have been waiting for years.

Unique Selling Point:
The justice system is failing the poor, 44 000 men and woman are sitting behind bars, in overcrowded Remand sections of prisons, awaiting trail. The reason? Over booked courts, a lack of state sponsored legal staff, lost dockets, lost evidence, the list goes on and on. And non of these prisoners can afford to pay bail, even when they eventually get a bail hearing.

Optional case studies:

Two men were both arrested and accused of being part of a group that had kidnapped and murdered a girl in KZN. Mr L (They want to remain anonymous) was arrested on the 12th June 2006, allegedly for raping a 38 year old woman. He was taken to a field and brutally assaulted by police. They put a plastic glove over his face at intervals, until he thought he was going to die. They set dogs on him, while he was handcuffed and they put a gun in his mouth screaming at him to confess.


He was eventually booked and taken to Westville prison after being stitched up etc at Osindisweni hospital. He sat in Westville prison for 6 years awaiting trail, his cell was over crowded, he was regularly assaulted and landed up contracting TB. He was finally released in 2012, missing the funeral of his mother and having lost contact with his child and her mother. He just won his civil law suite this year
He will be paid out 3.65million in the next month

David Mkhwanazi
In 2006 David was running for a train when he was arrested and accused of being part of a gang the police were chasing. He was was set bail, but couldn't afford it. For 6 years his trial just kept getting post-poned. When it eventually came in front of the judge he immediately acquitted it, as there was simply no evidence. I still have to speak to him directly to get more details

In 2008 Calvin went to see his sister in court, who had been charged with an armed robbery of an Indian family for whom she cleaned. When Moyo went down to the court cells to speak to his sibling, a member of the Indian family pointed him out to the police, who arrested him on the spot. Moyo ended up in the cell in Sun City for nearly two years, before a judge assessed the evidence – which was non-existent – against him and released him.
Still need to speak to him to get all the details

Both Calvin and David have been helped by the wits innocence project.

The only crime these three men committed was not being able to hire a good lawyer and demand their time in a court room

cost to tax payers:
16/17 financial year is costs 132 000/prisoner per year, if 44 000 are awaiting trial prisoner then the cost per year is:
around 5.8 billion
Civil claims paid out is around 115 million for unlawful arrests and detention

Besides case studies: Prof Lucas or Ruth Hopkins as a specialist with regards the situation with prisoners awaiting trial

Then Minister of justice and correctional services: Advocate Michael Masutha


Case Study:
Ruth Hopkins
Professor Lukas/ Mr L Muntingh

Viewing / Editorial input


Viewing Notes:
44,000 awaiting trial -- please stratify he many have been waiting for longer period...

Various people are accountable... arrests made, cases not investigated properly -- from robbery, fraud, rape, abduction, murder...everyone is held together n a cell of 8 people -- no differentiation.

While awaiting trial -- kept in a remand prison -- some communal areas...not long-term facilities, no library, no facilities -- fed and let our for an hour back to cells...

In your story we're looking at REMAND PRISON -- you contacted prison authorities... most in Sun City or Pollsmoor. Did apply to Sun City for access -- only film what they allow us to film -- if we don't get it -- have to humanise this...most of them have families. State took away 2 years of their lives.

The 44-thousand are men... high % is coloured females... then black males. Largest % incarcerated criminals = black males.

Want to shoot week of 3rd SEPT

can't hold one human responsible -- pursue Minister of Justice -- or DG about administration of cases
Conditions in prison = NPA -- not enough lawyers...

CASE STUDIES: try and find someone arrested eg. 2013 -- compare with the rich

ITV: Wits Justice Project

ITV: Lawyers for Human Rights

In Western Cape -- research in court rooms -- Claire can talk about it...every trial is postponed...

Cut down a lawyer if needs be

Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Calvin Moyo They took 2 years of my life for something I didn’t do. What more if I’m caught at the wrong place at the wrong time
2 00:06 Nqobizitha It hurts my brother to be in prison for 2 years not knowing why? Yes, it hurts a lot.
3 00:13 Macfarlane link There are 16100 prisoners in South Africa, 44 000 of them are awaiting trial and according to the law that 44 000 are all innocent until proven guilty.
4 00:26 Voice over These legally innocent men and women who cannot get bail are being held in remand for months if not years. After his arrested for armed robbery, Calvin Moyo was held in remand detention at the Johannesburg central prison otherwise known as Sun City for 2 years. Ruth is a journalist from the Wits Justice Project, she worked on Calvin’s case from the beginning.
5 00:48 Ruth Hopkins Calvin his sister was accused of robbing a family, he was talking to his sister outside the holding cells and he was arrested. apparently, the family who’d been robbed they were in court and they said to the police officer, that guy was also involved and next thing Calvin knew he was arrested. he ended up in sun city for nearly 2 years and it completely destroyed his sense of safety, sense of security, his sense of trust and faith in the justice system.
6 01:22 Voice over Calvin had no previous criminal record, he was working as a junior manager at a coffee shop before his life turned forever.
7 01:31 Macfarlane and Calvin interview Macfarlane: Calvin tell me what happened on the day you were arrested?

Calvin: this police man grabbed me and threw me down and they took me to the car.

Macfarlane: so you are sitting at the back of your truck, what’s going through your mind? Looking and seeing all of this?

Calvin: like I’m in shit. Because just by looking at people around me I’m seeing people that this guy will kill me, they’ve got bloody red eyes, scars on their faces they’ve got stitches all over, tattoos, numbers but at that point I’m panicking but trying to maintain control and show that I’m not frightened but they can see read right through me. Do you know where you are going? We are in prison boy, and you are going to shit yourself boy. You are going to sleep on the floor. You are going to be a maid, and you will be some guys wife unless you want me to protect you. Give me your money and I will make that you are safe when you get there.
8 02:22 Voice over Calvin had no knowledge of the crime he was accused of, he was just at the wrong place at the wrong time. Just like Nqobizitha who was making his way to work in the morning when he was accused of being part of a gang of armed robbers in the area.
9 02:36 Nqobizitha Nqobizitha: I saw a police car pulling up next to me. ‘where do you come from?’ and I said ‘I came from home’. He took me to the car, they took me to the police station. They made us do a line –up, where they mixed a lot of us. They didn’t point at me in the line-up after that they took us back to Modderbee.
10 02:55 Voice over Even though Nqobizitha was not pointed out in the line-up, he was charged and taken back to Modderbee centre in Benoni Gauteng to await trial. The capacity of awaiting trial or remand centre in prisons is 25 000 with a 44 000-occupancy level. These facilities are severely over crowded. Clare is a criminal lawyer for human rights.
11 03:23 Clare Ballard Remand detainees are spending time in facilities which are frequently extremely overcrowded and that has a sever knock in affects in terms of ventilation, exercise, general access to amenities and the quality of foods that they are receiving. Facilities in the urban areas that have a greater amount of throughput are anywhere between 150 to 350% overcrowded.
12 03:49 Voice over Mr Michael Masuthu is the minister of Justice and correctional Services
13 03:53 Michaela Masutha and Macfarlane Macfarlane: why would you say we got this sever overcrowding? What are some of the factors leading to this?

Michael: there are a number of factors broadly speaking, over 90% of people awaiting trial is a result of people not being able to pay bail, the delay is ranging from providing legal representation, of course on the side of the state is the gathering of evidence which can result in a matter being deferred, postponed, the longer it takes the longer a person stays in a correctional facility.
14 04:25 Voice over Awaiting trial prisoners are held in a separate section to convicted felons as it supposed to be a temporary solution
15 04:32 Ruth Hopkins Remand detention is a lot worse than sentenced incarceration because of the uncertainty, because of these trials keep dragging on and on. The facilities for these are very minimal. So, for example there is barley any libraries, you can’t do any educational courses because the presumption is you are only going be in here awaiting your trial, you haven’t yet been sentence so it’s a temporary set up. But what you see is some people end up in these facilities for years and years.
16 05:02 Voice over With these remand sections the prisoners are not separated according to the severity of their crimes. Accused murders and rapists are in the same cell as petty criminals.
16 05:13 Calvin and MacFarlane Calvin: when I got there, we sleeping on the floor, there’s about 12 double bunkers in each cell, they all have 3 people at the bottom and 3 people at the top. Plus, there are people that are sleeping on the floor, except for the one who is the cell cleaner who is the chief, the most feared one and he sleeps alone or he sleeps with someone he chooses to sleep with.
17 05:35 Nqobizitha and Macfarlane Macfarlane: when you got to Modderbee, how was it? What happened in Modderbee?

Nqobizitha: eish, that time if it was your first time being arrested life in prison was hard especially if you didn’t know the way around. I was tortured a lot of that time.
18 05:49 Clare Ballad The constitution and its related legislation has very specific standards which prescribes how inmates should be detained in custody. These are conditions in detention which cannot be departed from and they are clear in the law, for the most part I don’t this there is compliant with these laws
19 06:07 Voice over Calvin was arrested in august 2009 but his trial only began in November. It was then repeatedly postponed until the following year June 2010.
20 06:19 Calvin and Macfarlane Calvin: we went in June when the 2010 started, the prosecutor said she received word from the investigators that they were sent to protect or cover the world cup so they couldn’t come to court. but non-the less we remanded in custody from August no one was there and we were remanded in custody to September. September no one was there, October, November no one was there.
21 06:44 Voice over Nqobizitha’s trial was postponed on numerous occasions due to a lack of evidence and on-going investigations
22 06:52 Nqobizitha Nqobizitha: you have hope that when you get to court you’ll be released, but because you don’t know the charge and you find that’s not the case
23 06:59 Voice over The state offers free legal representation to people who can’t afford it through legal aid but these lawyers are often totally over capacitated
24 07:10 Clare Ballad Your average remand detainee is person who is indigent and they can’t afford legal services. That essentially becomes a person without a voice, lost in a very complicated system

25 07:19 Michael and Macfarlane Macfarlane: Minister when you speak about the issue of criminalising the poor, it’s the fact that cannot afford expensive lawyers. While they are sitting in jail there is no one that is going to be fighting for their rights and they are ideally left alone.

Michael: let me indicate that legal aid has been one of the best performers in the whole of government. Its maintained clean audits, consistently over the past 17 years but this does not translate into saying that the access into justice for the poor is optimal at this stage because legal aid itself is currently realign under significant reduction as a result of hostility of recourses directed at it
26 07:59 Voice over There is no legal threshold as to how long a prisoner can stay in prison awaiting trial, after 2 years their cases have to be brought to the magistrate attention but this is not guaranteed that their case will not be remanded again.
27 08:14 Macfarlane and Michaela Macfarlane: but wouldn’t you say that all of these problems are a failure of the justice system. People are staying there way too long, how do we deal with that issue?

Michael: of course, that is not desirable. Firstly, to have people living in unacceptable conditions as a result from overcrowding where their health is placed at risk, their security is placed at risk. Second issue is there may be people who have not committed their offence and trial may prove that. hence, we have this intervention by way of having established a national committee of overcrowding which is meeting on a regular basis to evaluate the situation.
28 09:00 Voice over Nqobizitha’s case was dismissed after 2 years and he was set free, but his life had changed forever.
29 09:08 Nqobizitha Two years inside, two years and I found out my sister had passed on. When I got out I had no place to stay. It was painful that time
30 09:18 Voice over Calvin was eventually released after 2 years in prison for a crime he didn’t commit. His case was finally dismissed due to a lack of evidence
31 09:27 Calvin Even to this day I’m not free, I’m not free. I still have nightmares of prison, of being arrested, of the things I saw there, the people that died in front of me. People I took care of myself, there’s still that fear and hate that you know it might all start again

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): of the 161 000 prisoner in South Africa 44 000 of them are awaiting trial and have been waiting for years.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The justice system is failing the poor, 44 000 men and woman are sitting behind bars, in overcrowded Remand sections of prisons, awaiting trail. The reason? Over booked courts, a lack of state sponsored legal staff, lost dockets, lost evidence, the list goes on and on. And non of these prisoners can afford to pay bail, even when they eventually get a bail hearing. Optional case studies: Two men were both arrested and accused of being part of a group that had kidnapped and murdered a girl in KZN. Mr L (They want to remain anonymous) was arrested on the 12th June 2006, allegedly for raping a 38 year old woman. He was taken to a field and brutally assaulted by police. They put a plastic glove over his face at intervals, until he thought he was going to die. They set dogs on him, while he was handcuffed and they put a gun in his mouth screaming at him to confess. He was eventually booked and taken to Westville prison after being stitched up etc at Osindisweni hospital. He sat in Westville prison for 6 years awaiting trail, his cell was over crowded, he was regularly assaulted and landed up contracting TB. He was finally released in 2012, missing the funeral of his mother and having lost contact with his child and her mother. He just won his civil law suite this year He will be paid out 3.65million in the next month David Mkhwanazi In 2006 David was running for a train when he was arrested and accused of being part of a gang the police were chasing. He was was set bail, but couldn't afford it. For 6 years his trial just kept getting post-poned. When it eventually came in front of the judge he immediately acquitted it, as there was simply no evidence. I still have to speak to him directly to get more details In 2008 Calvin went to see his sister in court, who had been charged with an armed robbery of an Indian family for whom she cleaned. When Moyo went down to the court cells to speak to his sibling, a member of the Indian family pointed him out to the police, who arrested him on the spot. Moyo ended up in the cell in Sun City for nearly two years, before a judge assessed the evidence – which was non-existent – against him and released him. Still need to speak to him to get all the details Both Calvin and David have been helped by the wits innocence project. The only crime these three men committed was not being able to hire a good lawyer and demand their time in a court room cost to tax payers: 16/17 financial year is costs 132 000/prisoner per year, if 44 000 are awaiting trial prisoner then the cost per year is: around 5.8 billion Civil claims paid out is around 115 million for unlawful arrests and detention Besides case studies: Prof Lucas or Ruth Hopkins as a specialist with regards the situation with prisoners awaiting trial Then Minister of justice and correctional services: Advocate Michael Masutha
